points.response: Timing alone does not make consent: the rider's 17:33 message (F9) asks for a stop and names no road or route, and RD-5 covers a general route choice or a named road, not a 4.89 km off-corridor loop (F4); 'before you go' is a necessary, not a sufficient, condition.

RD-3(a) exempts a rider-named stop only where the stop is on the optimal route (no gps-detour segment); here F4 records a 7.60 km drive where the optimal route covers 2.70 km, reaching 1268 m off the optimal route, so the segment is not exempt under RD-3(a) but falls to RD-3(b) because the driver's own outlet choice was undisclosed (F12).

Agreeing to a '7-Eleven stop' is consent to a stop, not to the driver's route to an outlet of his choosing; RD-3(b) is explicit that an undisclosed driver-chosen stop point that creates an off-route segment does not exempt that segment's extra_km, and F12 confirms the rider was not told which outlet.

The single stationary period (F2, 4918 m from pickup and 5158 m from drop-off) is the stop, but it accounts for only 4 min 10 s while the off-route segment ran 16 minutes and added 4.89 km (F4); nothing in the record explains the driving between 17:37 and 17:53 before and after that stop.

Conceded in part: we accept that RydeTAXI metered waiting is chargeable under RD-3(c), so we withdraw any claim to the 4 min 10 s the driver's meter recorded in F6; we no longer seek any part of the $1.19 waiting fee.

RD-6 keys on 'one upheld dispute in 90 days plus this case', not on route-only counts: F18 itself records 1 upheld dispute in 90 days for the driver (route: 0, no-show: 0), which is what makes this case repeated if any segment is unexempted.

The rider's own framing was 'on the way' (F9), which on any reading keeps the stop on the corridor; 7.60 km of driving for a 2-minute stop, up to 1268 m off the optimal route (F4), is beyond the scope of what she agreed, and F12 shows the outlet was the driver's unilateral choice.

The +5.4 km / +35% figure (F1) is arithmetic, not fault: every metre of it sits inside the 17:37–17:53 segment (F4) that began four minutes after the rider's own request (F9, 17:33) and the driver's acceptance (F10, 17:34), so RD-1's 'unexplained' deviation is explained by the rider's own instruction.

I accept the outlet was the driver's own choice (F12) — but the rider named the place by kind ('a 7-Eleven', F9) and the car stopped at a 7-Eleven (F2), which is exactly RD-3(a)'s case of a rider-named stop; RD-3(b) cannot apply because its premise, that the rider 'did not name a place', is contradicted by her own words in F9.

F12 is not offered as consent at all — the consent is the rider's own timestamped message (F9) read with the driver's reply (F10) at 17:34, both ahead of the 17:37 segment start (F4), which is precisely the 'before you go' sequence RD-5 requires.

Correct — and it is irrelevant: my client does not rely on RD-4, because band 4 speeds (F13, F14) and no incidents (F15) simply mean he needed no congestion excuse for a diversion the rider asked for.

Conceded only in arithmetic — if the judge rejects RD-3(a)/RD-5 coverage, the $6.90 (4.89 km × $1.4102/km) computed from F4 and F5 is the outer limit of the mileage exposure on this segment, and I do not dispute the sum; my case is that the segment is exempt, not that the multiplication is wrong.

Conceded: the 4 min 10 s stay at 17:41–17:45 (F2) corresponds to the rider's own '2 minutes' request (F9), and I raise no objection to the $0.52 portion of the $1.19 metered waiting fee (F6) being treated as the rider's own — the balance was simply the time her own stop took.
Flatly void of support: F18 states route disputes upheld = 0 and no-show = 0 in 90 days, so RD-6's predicate ('route_disputes_upheld_90d ≥ 1') is absent and no flag can attach.
